title: Bangladesh lost $2.26 billion to tax abuse in 2023, more than its health spending, says Tax Justice Network
excerpt: The State of Tax Justice 2026 report says multinationals accounted for $2.18 billion of the loss. The total equals 161% of government health spending.

image.alt: The National Board of Revenue building in Dhaka
image.credit: File photo: Yahya / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
Bangladesh lost an estimated $2.26 billion in tax revenue in 2023 to cross-border tax abuse by multinational companies and wealthy individuals, according to the Tax Justice Network's State of Tax Justice 2026 report released on Tuesday (24 November), The Business Standard reported.

According to the report, as reported by The Business Standard, multinational companies shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions accounted for $2.18 billion, or about 96.5%, of the loss. The remaining $79 million came from wealthy individuals hiding assets offshore.

The total loss equalled 161% of the government's health spending in 2023, and the corporate share alone 156%, the report said. It was also equal to 91% of a year's average wages for all unemployed young people aged 15 to 24 in Bangladesh. Bangladesh had the second-largest loss in South Asia after India ($34.22 billion), ahead of Pakistan ($1.33 billion) and Sri Lanka ($624.4 million).

Globally, the Tax Justice Network estimated that countries lost $475 billion in corporate tax in 2023, and at least $108.5 billion to offshore tax abuse by individuals, more than four times the $26 billion in international public finance that developing countries received that year to adapt to climate change. The network called for a fully inclusive system of tax cooperation under the proposed UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, whose negotiations are due to end in July 2027.

Towfiqul Islam Khan, head of research at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), told The Business Standard that the government should strengthen the tax administration's capacity, speed up digitisation and tackle corruption. "Tax policies should be based on objective assessments and distributional justice rather than ad hoc decisions or the influence of vested interests," he said. He added that these reforms should feature in talks with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.

Devlens has not seen the Bangladesh country figures in the report itself; the figures above are as reported by The Business Standard.

Why it matters

With aid falling, the revenue the state collects at home matters more for health, education and social protection. Estimates like these give civil society groups working on tax justice and budget advocacy a figure to set against spending on public services.

What to watch

  • Bangladesh's position in the UN tax convention negotiations.
  • Revenue measures in talks with the IMF and in the next budget.
  • Any government response to the transfer-pricing figures.

Sources

  • The Business Standard: Bangladesh lost $2.26b to tax abuse in 2023 alone, global study finds, 26 November 2026
  • Tax Justice Network: The State of Tax Justice 2026, November 2026
